cheribsd-revocation.oracle: MEASURED 2026-10-09, results/2026-10-09-cheribsd/: **NO FAULT, AND NO REUSE.** The sequence completes with aliased=0: the stale pointer was followed, but the chunk it names was never handed to another allocation, because CheriBSD's libc holds a released chunk in QUARANTINE until the revoker has swept every capability to it. So the access reads only the dead object -- the exploitable half of a use-after-free, reading or writing SOMEONE ELSE'S object, did not happen. It is not a fault, because nothing forced a sweep between the free and the access: the stale capability still carried its tag, as the case was built to leave it. revocation control in the same boot: revocation=1 tag_after_sweep=0 reissued=1, then SIGPROT si_code 2 at the control's own probe, so the revoker demonstrably acts in this guest and a completion here is the mechanism's design, not an inactive mechanism. CONTRAST, measured in the sibling nested corpora: there the inner allocator reissues the storage at once and the stale pointer DOES read another object, because nothing reaches free(). Predicted before the run; the prediction held.
cheribsd-revocation.platform: stock CheriBSD purecap, kernel CHERI-PURECAP-QEMU, revocation ON (--runtime-revocation on); cheribsd-abi, cheribsd-bounds and the revocation control all PASSED in the same boot.

native-detect.oracle: the buggy arm's stale pointer reads or writes storage that now belongs to a different live object, and the case's aliasing flag is set; under the fix the pointer is cleared or the iteration is skipped, so nothing aliases. The arms differ by the upstream fix, not by protection. ASan reports heap-use-after-free at the labelled probe on the buggy arm and is silent on the fixed arm -- keyed on heap-use-after-free, never on the string AddressSanitizer, which LeakSanitizer's summary also matches.

title: a flush flag was written into a watcher the poll it had just called may have freed
object: a log watcher, one calloc(1, sizeof(logger_watcher))
lifetime_ender: free(w) inside logger_thread_close_watcher, reached from logger_thread_poll_watchers
shape: a helper that may free the object its caller is standing on
allocator_layer: the platform allocator itself: one direct malloc/calloc/getline allocation, with neither memcached suballocator in the path.
fidelity: model consumer, real lifetime: the allocation, the free and the later access through the stale pointer are upstream's, quoted in PROVENANCE.md. The later access is `w->failed_flush = true;`, a WRITE into the freed watcher.
status: built 2026-10-08; native arms measured by runners/run-native.sh in the same commit. The platform arms are declared predictions. CheriBSD measured 2026-10-09 (results/2026-10-09-cheribsd/): NOT-REISSUED.
live_proof: absent at the pin: this fix was SUPERSEDED by 3bc58f6ea55a rather than reverted, so `grep -c 'if (watchers[x] != NULL) {'` on 1.6.45:logger.c is 0 while the successor's `if (watchers[x] == NULL) {` appears twice. The unguarded write is at e7793811f8c8^ and is absent from the pin. A fix-reversal.
nested_why: the object came straight from malloc / calloc / getline, with neither slabs.c nor cache.c between it and the request. So under this inventory's axis, WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT, this row is NOT nested. Its sibling ../allocator-repros holds the nested ones.
distinguishing: the free is two calls deep and CONDITIONAL on the peer having gone away, so nothing at the write's own line suggests the object might be gone -- the fix's own comment is the documentation: 'Oddity; poll_watchers can free *w, recheck it.' The close also nulls the global slot `watchers[w->id]` but cannot null the caller's local `w`, which is what leaves the dangling pointer.
